planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in full sun on moist, well-drained soil; shelter young trees from harsh wind and hard freezes until the trunk has hardened off.

directions: Native to the floodplain forests of southwestern Turkey and Rhodes, this is a much smaller and more compact relative of American sweetgum, usually forming a broad, egg-shaped crown of horizontal to slightly pendulous branches well under forty feet tall. Its star-shaped leaves turn shades of yellow, orange, and purple-red in fall, though the display is often subtler than that of the American species. Give it full sun on fertile, moist but well-drained, neutral to acidic soil, and site it with some protection from strong winter wind since young growth can be frost-tender. It tolerates occasional wet or flooded ground better than most sweetgums, reflecting its native swampy habitat.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil; this montane Chinese species is hardier than it looks and tolerates average garden winters once established.

directions: Collected from montane forests of central and southern China, this sweetgum is grown chiefly for foliage that opens a striking burgundy-red in spring before settling to deep green through summer and flaring back into red and purple tones each autumn. It grows into an upright, conical to rounded small-to-medium shade tree, generally more compact than American sweetgum. Plant in full sun to part shade on fertile, moist, well-drained soil, and shelter it somewhat from drying wind while young. It is still uncommon outside specialty and arboretum collections but has proven reliably hardy well into cool-temperate gardens.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, including alkaline sites; this Mexican native handles heat and drought far better than American sycamore but is less cold-hardy.

directions: Widely planted as a fast-growing shade and accent tree across the warmer Southwest, Mexican sycamore is prized for its smooth, mottled gray-white bark and large, lobed leaves with silvery, felted undersides that flash in the wind. It is notably more drought-tolerant than American sycamore and resists the bacterial leaf scorch that often disfigures its northern relative in hot climates. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, including alkaline ground where many other large shade trees struggle, and give it room since it quickly reaches a substantial mature size. It is best suited to milder winters, as hard freezes can injure young wood.
